name: Brill's Time-Symmetric Gravitational Waves
description: One moment of a spacetime that holds gravitational waves and nothing else, which Dieter Brill constructed in 1959. It is a single slice of space, three dimensions with no time, at the moment the wave is at rest, and it satisfies Einstein's constraint equations with no matter anywhere. Brill proved its mass positive, a strong enough wave already lies inside its own apparent horizon, and what the wave does afterwards is known from computer simulations.
convention: Every coordinate is spatial, so no component carries a factor of $c$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to arc length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. A mass $M$ enters as the length $GM/c^2$.
history:
Dieter Brill made a "still photograph" of a gravitational wave in 1959, his own name for it: one moment of a spacetime with waves in it and nothing else [brill1959]. He made it to settle whether such a wave weighs anything, since on "some views that question the reality of gravitational radiation", as he put it, the mass of a spacetime with no sources "will always be zero" [brill1959]. Hermann Bondi had already found the energy positive to second order in the strength of the wave, for waves in the shape of a doughnut that Joseph Weber and John Wheeler had considered [brill1959]. Could it be shown with no approximation?¶A whole spacetime full of waves is hard to find, and one moment of it is much easier [cook2000]. Choose the moment at which the wave is at rest, as a pendulum is at the top of its swing, so that its history reads the same forward and backward from there [cook2000]. Einstein's equations then put one condition on that slice of space, that its scalar curvature vanish [cook2000]. For a wave symmetric about an axis Brill wrote the slice as $$ds^2 = \psi^4\left[e^{2q}\left(dho^2 + dz^2ight) + ho^2 d\phi^2ight],$$ and the condition is one linear equation for $\psi$, $$
abla^2\psi + 	frac{1}{4}\left(\partial_ho^2 q + \partial_z^2 qight)\psi = 0,$$ with $
abla^2$ the Laplacian of flat space [brill1959, omurchadha1993]. The function $q(ho, z)$ is the shape of the wave, and any $q$ will do that vanishes on the axis and dies away far off [omurchadha1993].¶Far from the wave the slice looks like the space around a mass $M$, with $\psi 	o 1 + GM/2c^2r$ [omurchadha1993]. Brill found that $$ rac{GM}{c^2} =  rac{1}{2\pi}\int\left( rac{
abla\psi}{\psi}ight)^2 dV,$$ the integral of a square over flat space [brill1959, omurchadha1993]. So the wave has a positive mass whatever its shape and however strong it is, and the mass vanishes only for flat space [brill1959, omurchadha1993]. Niall Ó Murchadha called this "the first positivity of energy result in General Relativity" [omurchadha1993]. The theorem for every isolated system waited twenty years, until Richard Schoen and Shing-Tung Yau proved it, and Edward Witten found a second proof two years after theirs [schoen1979, witten1981].¶How strong can the wave be made? With the shape $q$ fixed and its amplitude turned up, the equation for $\psi$ is the one a quantum particle obeys as it scatters at zero energy off a potential well, which is how Wheeler read it in 1964 [wheeler1964, omurchadha1993]. A deep enough well traps the particle, and at that amplitude $\psi$ and the mass grow without bound [omurchadha1993]. Kenneth Eppley, who pioneered solving for $\psi$ on a computer, saw two stages in 1977: "The initial data contain a black hole if the amplitude of the waves is sufficiently strong", and "At a critical amplitude the throat pinches off and the geometry becomes singular" [eppley1977, omurchadha1993]. Trapped surfaces appear as that amplitude is approached, by a theorem of Robert Beig and Ó Murchadha's from 1991, so a strong enough wave sits inside a horizon already in the photograph [beig1991, omurchadha1993]. At the critical amplitude itself the slice closes up into a universe with no outside and nothing in it but the wave [omurchadha1993].¶Most computations since have used one wave, $q = aho^2e^{-r^2}$ with $r^2 = ho^2 + z^2$ and every length in units of the wave's width, which Daniel Holz, Warner Miller, Masami Wakano, and Wheeler introduced in 1993 [holz1993, hilditch2017]. Seven years on Miguel Alcubierre and six coauthors solved it again, with two solvers for $\psi$ and three ways of finding a horizon [alcubierre2000]. Their masses agree with Holz's, $GM/c^2 = 0.70$ at $a = 5$ and $4.67$ at $a = 12$, but their first apparent horizon appears at an amplitude between $11.81$ and $11.82$, where Holz and his coauthors had reported $7.5$ [alcubierre2000]. For Eppley's wave they found masses that differ from his, and at the amplitude where he had seen the throat pinch off they saw nothing of the kind [alcubierre2000].¶What the wave does after the photograph had to be computed, and Alcubierre, Gabrielle Allen, Bernd Brügmann, Gerd Lanfermann, Edward Seidel, Wai-Mo Suen, and Malcolm Tobias followed Holz's wave in three dimensions [alcubierre2000collapse]. At $a = 4$ it falls in on itself, bounces a few times, and disperses, leaving flat space [alcubierre2000collapse]. At $a = 6$ it collapses to a black hole of mass $0.87$ and radiates the remaining $0.12$ of its $0.99$ away [alcubierre2000collapse]. The threshold between the two fates lies far below the amplitude at which the photograph first shows a horizon: David Hilditch, Andreas Weyhausen, and Brügmann placed it between $a = 4.6966875$ and $4.696703125$ in 2017 [hilditch2017]. Just above such a threshold, for a different family of waves, Andrew Abrahams and Charles Evans had found black holes whose masses follow a power law with an exponent near $0.37$ [abrahams1993, hilditch2013]. For Brill's waves the law is still unconfirmed, and Hilditch and his coauthors call their evidence for it "not conclusive" [hilditch2017].

related.text: The same kind of moment with black holes in it. Set $q = 0$ and give $\psi$ poles, and Brill's slice becomes the one he and Richard Lindquist built in 1963 for two holes at rest [brill1963, cook2000].
The wave gone quiet. With $q = 0$ the only regular $\psi$ that goes to $1$ far away is $1$ itself, and the slice is a moment of Minkowski's flat spacetime [brill1959].
Gravitational waves with cylindrical fronts, known exactly for all time. Weber and Wheeler argued for their reality in 1957, two years before Brill weighed his [weber1957, brill1959].

Far from the wave the slice approaches that of Schwarzschild's mass at the moment $t = 0$, in isotropic coordinates [alcubierre2000, cook2000]. A wave strong enough to collapse leaves a black hole behind [alcubierre2000collapse].

One more moment of time symmetry: a closed universe of dust behind a throat. A Brill wave turned up to its critical amplitude closes off as well, into a compact universe with nothing in it but the wave [omurchadha1993].

A scalar field on the threshold between dispersing and collapsing to a black hole, in closed form. Brill's waves have the same two fates, with the threshold of Holz's wave at $a = 4.70$ [hilditch2017].
Wheeler's geon was a ball of waves held together by its own gravity, mass without matter [wheeler1955]. Brill and James Hartle built the geon of gravitational waves in 1964 [brillhartle1964].
Dieter Brill's closed universe of 1964, a whole spacetime "filled with gravitational and electromagnetic radiation" and nothing else [brill1964].
